draft.title: Land rights and native title
card: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, land is more than property. It is tied to the Dreaming, to kinship and to ceremony, so a connection to Country is spiritual as well as legal.

In 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) that the Meriam people of the Torres Strait held rights to their land under their own law and custom. It rejected the idea that Australia was terra nullius, meaning land belonging to no one.

The Commonwealth Parliament passed this law after Mabo. It set up a process to recognise native title, which is the rights and interests in land that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples hold under their own laws and customs.

Native title can be recognised only where a group has kept its connection to the land and the connection has not been extinguished by other laws or actions. So it recognises some connections to land, not all of them.
draft.remember: Mabo and the Native Title Act recognised some connections to land that are spiritual as well as legal.

a.q: What did the High Court decide in the Mabo decision of 1992?
opts: Rights to land can exist under Indigenous law and custom
All land in Australia was returned to Aboriginal peoples
Land rights depend on a group belonging to a church
Native title was created by the Native Title Act 1993
a.why: The Court found that rights to land under Indigenous law and custom could survive, and it rejected terra nullius. It did not return all land. The Native Title Act came after Mabo, so it did not create the idea.
a.clue: The Court recognised rights that already existed under Indigenous law.

b.q: An Aboriginal group applies for native title over land that holds its sacred sites. Why is the Native Title Act 1993 important to its spiritual life?
opts: It can legally recognise a spiritual connection to Country
It guarantees the group ownership of all land in its region
It makes the group's ceremonies a recognised religion in law
It ends any need to show a continuing connection to the land
b.why: The Act can recognise rights and interests that come from a group's own laws and customs, which include spiritual ties to Country. It does not guarantee all land, because the connection must have continued and not been extinguished. The tempting option about all land ignores that limit.
b.clue: Native title recognises some connections, and the group must show its own.

a.best: Rights to land can exist under Indigenous law and custom

b.best: It can legally recognise a spiritual connection to Country

problems.detail: The first bullet ties the land connection of both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to 'the Dreaming'. The Dreaming is an Aboriginal concept. Torres Strait Islander spiritualities, including those of the Meriam people in the Mabo case, are distinct (for example Ailan Kastom). The card should not apply the Dreaming to Torres Strait Islander peoples.
The clue 'The Court recognised rights that already existed under Indigenous law' nearly restates the right option, so it gives the answer away.

The right option is the only one with the qualifier 'can'. The other three are absolute ('guarantees', 'ends any need', 'makes'), so a student can pick it without knowing the idea. The clue 'recognises some connections' points the same way.

check.summary: The facts about Mabo and the Native Title Act are correct, but the card wrongly links Torres Strait Islander peoples to the Dreaming. The clue for question a gives the answer away, and the right option in question b stands out as the only qualified one.

proposal.title: Land rights and native title
card: For Aboriginal peoples, land is tied to the Dreaming, to kinship and to ceremony. Torres Strait Islander peoples have their own distinct spiritual ties to land and sea, known as Ailan Kastom (island custom). For both, a connection to land is spiritual as well as legal.

In 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) that the Meriam people of the Torres Strait held rights to their land under their own law and custom. It rejected the idea that Australia was terra nullius, meaning land belonging to no one.

The Commonwealth Parliament passed this law after Mabo. It set up a process to recognise native title, which is the rights and interests in land that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples hold under their own laws and customs.

Native title can be recognised only where a group has kept its connection to the land and the connection has not been extinguished by other laws or actions. So it recognises some connections to land, not all of them.
proposal.remember: Mabo and the Native Title Act recognised some connections to land that are spiritual as well as legal.

a.q: What did the High Court decide in the Mabo decision of 1992?
opts: Rights to land under traditional law had survived
All land in Australia was handed back to Indigenous peoples
Land rights depended on a group belonging to a church
Native title had been created by the Native Title Act
a.why: The Court found that the Meriam people's rights under their own law and custom had survived, and it rejected terra nullius. It did not hand back all land. The Native Title Act came after Mabo, so it could not have been the source of the Court's ruling.
a.clue: Check which came first, the ruling or the Act.

b.q: An Aboriginal group applies for native title over land that holds its sacred sites. Why is the Native Title Act 1993 important to its spiritual life?
opts: It provides a legal way to recognise ties to Country
It gives the group ownership of all land in its region
It declares the group's ceremonies a religion in law
It removes the need to show a continuing connection
b.why: The Act set up a process to recognise rights that come from a group's own laws and customs, which include spiritual ties to Country. It does not give ownership of all land in a region, because the connection must have continued and not been extinguished. That limit also rules out the option about removing the need to show a connection.
b.clue: Think about what the Act set up after Mabo.
